items.definition: To throw someone or something out of a window; figuratively, to remove someone abruptly from a position.
items.etymology: From Latin de 'down from' and fenestra 'window', coined after the Defenestration of Prague in 1618.
items.example_sentence: The board moved to defenestrate the chief executive after the scandal.

items.definition: Having a ready insight into things; shrewd and quick to understand.
items.etymology: From Latin perspicax 'sharp-sighted', from perspicere 'to look through'.
items.example_sentence: A perspicacious editor spotted the flaw in the argument at once.

items.definition: Using long words, or characterised by long words.
items.etymology: From Latin sesquipedalis 'a foot and a half long', a joke by the poet Horace about long words.
items.example_sentence: His sesquipedalian prose made the manual hard to follow.

items.definition: Looking or sounding sad and dismal, often to an exaggerated degree.
items.etymology: From Latin lugubris 'mournful', from lugere 'to mourn'.
items.example_sentence: The cellist played a lugubrious melody as the credits rolled.

items.definition: A soft whispering or rustling sound.
items.etymology: From Latin susurrus 'a whisper', an imitation of the sound.
items.example_sentence: The susurrus of the wind in the pines put her to sleep.

items.definition: Relating to twilight; in zoology, active mainly at dawn and dusk.
items.etymology: From Latin crepusculum 'twilight'.
items.example_sentence: Deer are crepuscular, so drive carefully at dusk.

items.definition: The pleasant earthy smell that comes with the first rain after a dry spell.
items.etymology: Coined in 1964 by two Australian chemists from Greek petra 'stone' and ichor, the fluid in the veins of the gods.
items.example_sentence: After weeks of drought, the petrichor drifted in through the open window.

items.definition: The warmth of the sun on a cold winter day.
items.etymology: From Latin apricitas 'sunniness', from apricus 'exposed to the sun'; recorded in English in the 1620s.
items.example_sentence: They ate lunch on the bench, grateful for the apricity of the January noon.

items.definition: Physical beauty; a formal or humorous word.
items.etymology: From Latin pulchritudo, from pulcher 'beautiful'.
items.example_sentence: The travel guide praised the pulchritude of the coastline.

items.definition: Noisy and difficult to control.
items.etymology: From Latin obstreperus 'clamorous', from ob 'against' and strepere 'to make a noise'.
items.example_sentence: The obstreperous fans were escorted out of the stadium.

items.definition: Serving no practical purpose; superfluous.
items.etymology: From Latin otiosus 'at leisure', from otium 'leisure'.
items.example_sentence: Half of the clauses in the old policy were otiose and could be deleted.

items.definition: To keep changing one's stated opinion; to equivocate.
items.etymology: From Latin tergiversari 'to turn one's back', from tergum 'back' and vertere 'to turn'.
items.example_sentence: The minister continued to tergiversate on the question of taxes.

items.definition: A rumbling or gurgling noise made by gas moving in the intestines.
items.etymology: From Greek borborygmos, an imitation of the sound.
items.example_sentence: An embarrassing borborygmus broke the silence of the exam hall.

items.definition: Sweet or musical; pleasant to hear.
items.etymology: From Latin mellifluus 'flowing with honey', from mel 'honey' and fluere 'to flow'.
items.example_sentence: The narrator's mellifluous voice made the audiobook a pleasure.

items.definition: Showing a lack of courage or determination; timid.
items.etymology: From Latin pusillanimis, from pusillus 'very small' and animus 'mind, spirit'.
items.example_sentence: Critics called the decision to drop the investigation pusillanimous.

items.definition: A person who is devoted to luxury and pleasure.
items.etymology: From Sybaris, an ancient Greek city in Italy famous for its luxury.
items.example_sentence: The resort caters to sybarites who expect champagne at breakfast.

items.definition: Of or occurring every day; ordinary or everyday.
items.etymology: From Latin quotidianus, from quotidie 'daily'.
items.example_sentence: The novel finds beauty in quotidian routines like making coffee.

items.definition: Little known; requiring specialised or obscure knowledge.
items.etymology: From Latin reconditus 'hidden', from recondere 'to put away'.
items.example_sentence: The lecture wandered into recondite details of medieval tax law.

items.definition: Winding or circuitous; full of twists.
items.etymology: From Latin anfractuosus, from anfractus 'a bending'.
items.example_sentence: The anfractuous coastal road doubled the driving time.

items.definition: A change of circumstances, typically one that is unwelcome or unpleasant.
items.etymology: From Latin vicissitudo, from vicissim 'in turn'.
items.example_sentence: The family business survived the vicissitudes of three recessions.

items.definition: A tendency to talk at great length, often incoherently.
items.etymology: From Greek logos 'word' and rhoia 'flow', modelled on diarrhea.
items.example_sentence: The panel's moderator struggled to contain one guest's logorrhea.

items.definition: Composure or coolness under pressure.
items.etymology: From French sang-froid 'cold blood'.
items.example_sentence: The pilot landed the damaged plane with remarkable sangfroid.

items.definition: A gap or missing portion, especially in a text or in knowledge.
items.etymology: From Latin lacuna 'pool, hole', from lacus 'lake'.
items.example_sentence: The study fills a lacuna in research on adult language learning.

items.definition: A manuscript page scraped and reused; anything with layers of earlier forms still visible.
items.etymology: From Greek palimpsestos 'scraped again', from palin 'again' and psen 'to scrape'.
items.example_sentence: The old city is a palimpsest of Roman, medieval and modern streets.

items.definition: Deceitful and untrustworthy; betraying trust.
items.etymology: From Latin perfidiosus, from perfidia 'treachery', from per fidem decipere 'to deceive through trust'.
items.example_sentence: The perfidious ally switched sides on the eve of battle.

items.definition: Of no value or importance; also, having no force.
items.etymology: From Latin nugatorius 'worthless', from nugae 'trifles'.
items.example_sentence: The savings from the change were nugatory compared with its cost.

items.definition: Using or containing too many words; tediously long.
items.etymology: From Latin prolixus 'poured out, extended'.
items.example_sentence: The prolix report buried its single recommendation on page forty.

items.definition: Not self-indulgent, especially in eating and drinking.
items.etymology: From Latin abstemius, from abs 'from' and temetum 'strong drink'.
items.example_sentence: An abstemious diet kept the old monk healthy into his nineties.

items.definition: Gigantic; enormous in size or scale, like the giants of Swift's satire.
items.etymology: From Brobdingnag, the land of giants in Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726).
items.example_sentence: The new data centre has brobdingnagian cooling towers.

items.definition: In a direction contrary to the sun's course; counterclockwise.
items.etymology: From Middle Low German weddersinnes 'against the way'.
items.example_sentence: Folklore warned against walking widdershins around a church.

items.definition: A confused jumble or medley of things.
items.etymology: From French galimafrée, a kind of stew or ragout.
items.example_sentence: The attic held a gallimaufry of toys, tools and old letters.

items.definition: A person who gives opinions on matters beyond their knowledge.
items.etymology: From Latin ultra crepidam 'beyond the sandal', after a painter's advice to a cobbler to judge only the shoes.
items.example_sentence: The comment section filled with ultracrepidarians explaining virology.

items.definition: A wish or inclination too weak to lead to action.
items.etymology: From Medieval Latin velleitas, from Latin velle 'to wish'.
items.example_sentence: Learning the cello remained a velleity rather than a plan.

items.definition: Glowing or flickering softly; also, lightly brilliant, as of wit.
items.etymology: From Latin lambere 'to lick', of flames that seem to lick a surface.
items.example_sentence: The lambent glow of the candles softened the room.

items.definition: To flash or sparkle; figuratively, to be brilliantly witty.
items.etymology: From Latin coruscare 'to glitter'.
items.example_sentence: Sunlight coruscated on the waves below the cliff.

items.definition: Shining brightly; radiant.
items.etymology: From Latin effulgere 'to shine out', from ex 'out' and fulgere 'to shine'.
items.example_sentence: An effulgent sunrise lit the snowfields gold.

items.definition: To persuade someone to do something by flattery or deception.
items.etymology: From Anglo-Norman envegler 'to blind', from Old French aveugler.
items.example_sentence: He inveigled his way into the private reception.

items.definition: Not telling the truth; lying.
items.etymology: From Latin mendax 'lying', from mentiri 'to lie'.
items.example_sentence: The investigation exposed a mendacious account of the accident.

items.definition: A long and meandering journey, especially on foot or abroad.
items.etymology: From Latin peregrinatio, from peregrinus 'foreign, from abroad'.
items.example_sentence: Her peregrinations across Central Asia filled three notebooks.

items.definition: A sequence of real or imagined images, like those in a dream.
items.etymology: From French fantasmagorie, an 1802 name for a magic-lantern show, from Greek phantasma 'image'.
items.example_sentence: The festival was a phantasmagoria of lanterns, masks and music.

items.definition: Unattractive and objectionable; off-putting.
items.etymology: From French rébarbatif, from se rebarber 'to face each other beard to beard'.
items.example_sentence: The building's rebarbative concrete facade divided critics.

items.definition: The view that only one's own mind is sure to exist; extreme self-centredness.
items.etymology: From Latin solus 'alone' and ipse 'self'.
items.example_sentence: The memoir's solipsism left little room for anyone else's perspective.

items.definition: A song, poem or lament of mourning.
items.etymology: From Greek threnoidia, from threnos 'wailing' and oide 'song'.
items.example_sentence: The orchestra closed the memorial with a threnody for strings.

items.definition: Bitter and abusive language.
items.etymology: From Latin vituperatio, from vituperare 'to blame', from vitium 'fault'.
items.example_sentence: The debate descended into vituperation on both sides.

items.definition: The highest point in the development of something; a perfect example; also, deification.
items.etymology: From Greek apotheosis, from apotheoun 'to make a god of', from theos 'god'.
items.example_sentence: Many critics see the final symphony as the apotheosis of his style.

items.definition: To remove material considered improper from a text, often weakening it.
items.etymology: From Thomas Bowdler, who published an expurgated Shakespeare in 1818.
items.example_sentence: The school edition bowdlerized the play's most famous jokes.

items.definition: Stubbornly or wilfully disobedient to authority.
items.etymology: From Latin contumax 'insolent, stubborn'.
items.example_sentence: The contumacious witness refused to answer the court's questions.

items.definition: Relating to or dependent on charity.
items.etymology: From Medieval Latin eleemosynarius, from eleemosyna 'alms', from Greek eleos 'mercy'.
items.example_sentence: The hospital began as an eleemosynary institution run by monks.

items.definition: Mental dullness or lethargy.
items.etymology: From Latin hebetudo, from hebes 'blunt, dull'.
items.example_sentence: The heat produced a hebetude that no amount of coffee could lift.

items.definition: Naive and simplistic; also, dull and lacking in substance.
items.etymology: From Latin jejunus 'fasting, barren'.
items.example_sentence: His jejune analysis ignored every complicating factor.

items.definition: Government by the least qualified or most unprincipled citizens.
items.etymology: From Greek kakistos 'worst' and kratos 'rule'; first recorded in 1829.
items.example_sentence: The satirist described the council as a kakistocracy.

items.definition: Laborious study or meditation, originally by lamplight; also a pedantic piece of writing.
items.etymology: From Latin lucubratio, from lucubrare 'to work by lamplight', from lux 'light'.
items.example_sentence: Years of lucubration produced a thousand-page commentary.

items.definition: A person who has or claims a great deal of authority or influence.
items.etymology: From the Grand Panjandrum, a nonsense title invented by the playwright Samuel Foote in 1755.
items.example_sentence: The company's panjandrums approved the budget without reading it.

items.definition: The inherent nature or essence of something; also, a trivial objection.
items.etymology: From Medieval Latin quidditas, from Latin quid 'what'.
items.example_sentence: The essay tries to capture the quiddity of a New York summer.

items.definition: Boastful or inflated talk or behaviour.
items.etymology: From Rodomonte, a boastful king in Italian epics by Boiardo and Ariosto.
items.example_sentence: Behind the rodomontade, the team had no real plan.

items.definition: Showing great or excessive fondness for one's wife.
items.etymology: From Latin uxorius, from uxor 'wife'.
items.example_sentence: The uxorious king granted his queen every wish.

items.definition: A soft, gentle breeze.
items.etymology: From Greek Zephyros, the god of the west wind.
items.example_sentence: A warm zephyr stirred the curtains on the balcony.

items.definition: To misappropriate money held in trust; to embezzle.
items.etymology: From Medieval Latin defalcare 'to lop off', from falx 'sickle'.
items.example_sentence: The treasurer was found to have defalcated funds from the club account.

items.definition: Inclined to cause or undergo division into separate parts or groups.
items.etymology: From Latin fissus 'split' and parere 'to bring forth'.
items.example_sentence: The fissiparous coalition split into four parties within a year.

items.definition: To talk or move in a rambling, aimless way.
items.etymology: Perhaps from obsolete maunder 'to beg'; origin uncertain.
items.example_sentence: He maundered on about his holiday long after everyone had stopped listening.
